claim: The T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire encodes immune exposure history through the dynamic formation of immunological memory.
source: The T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire encodes immune exposure history through the dynamic formation of immunological memory.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about TCR repertoires presented in the abstract as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Statistical analysis of repertoire sequencing data has the potential to decode disease associations from large cohorts with measured phenotypes.
source: Statistical analysis of repertoire sequencing data has the potential to decode disease associations from large cohorts with measured phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's approach and is presented as a motivation for the research.

claim: The repertoire perturbation induced by a given immunological challenge is conditioned on genetic background via major histocompatibility complex (MHC) polymorphism.
source: However, the repertoire perturbation induced by a given immunological challenge is conditioned on genetic background via major histocompatibility complex (MHC) polymorphism.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the relationship between MHC and TCR repertoires.

claim: The analysis reveals striking imprints of common pathogens in TCR occurrence patterns.
source: our analysis reveals rich structure: striking imprints of common pathogens
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of the cohort data.

claim: The analysis identifies clusters of co-occurring TCRs that may represent markers of shared immune exposures.
source: clusters of co-occurring TCRs that may represent markers of shared immune exposures
evidence: This is a primary finding from the clustering analysis performed in the study.

claim: There are substantial variations in TCR-MHC association strength across MHC loci.
source: substantial variations in TCR-MHC association strength across MHC loci
evidence: This finding is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5 comparing association rates across different HLA loci.

claim: There is sequence covariation between TCR and MHC that is guided by atomic contacts in solved TCR:peptide-MHC structures.
source: Guided by atomic contacts in solved TCR:peptide-MHC structures, we identify sequence covariation between TCR and MHC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis presented in the study.

claim: T cells are the effectors of cell-mediated adaptive immunity in jawed vertebrates.
source: T cells are the effectors of cell-mediated adaptive immunity in jawed vertebrates.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge presented in the introduction.

claim: Massive genetic diversity in loci encoding the T cell receptor (TCR) is generated somatically throughout an individual's life via a process called V(D)J recombination.
source: To control a broad array of pathogens, massive genetic diversity in loci encoding the T cell receptor (TCR) is generated somatically throughout an individual's life via a process called V(D)J recombination.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TCR diversity generation.

claim: All nucleated cells regularly process and present internal peptide antigens on cell surface molecules called major histocompatibility complex (MHC).
source: All nucleated cells regularly process and present internal peptide antigens on cell surface molecules called major histocompatibility complex (MHC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about antigen presentation.

claim: A T cell with a TCR having affinity for a peptide antigen complexed with MHC (pMHC) is stimulated to initiate an immune response to an infected (or cancerous) cell.
source: Through the interface of TCR and MHC, a T cell with a TCR having affinity for a peptide antigen complexed with MHC (pMHC) is stimulated to initiate an immune response to an infected (or cancerous) cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T cell activation.

claim: The responding T cell proliferates clonally, and its progeny inherit the same antigen-specific TCR, constituting long-term immunological memory of the antigen.
source: The responding T cell proliferates clonally, and its progeny inherit the same antigen-specific TCR, constituting long-term immunological memory of the antigen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T cell clonal expansion and memory formation.

claim: Public TCRs have been found in a range of infectious and autoimmune diseases and cancers including influenza, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus infections, type I diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and melanoma.
source: Public TCRs—defined as TCR sequences seen in multiple individuals and perhaps associated with a shared disease phenotype—have been found in a range of infectious and autoimmune diseases and cancers including influenza, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus infections, type I diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and melanoma (Venturi et al., 2008; Li et al., 2012; Madi et al., 2017; Pogorelyy et al., 2017; Dash et al., 2017; Glanville et al., 2017; Chu et al., 2018; Pogorelyy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Emerson et al. identified a set of CMV-associated TCR chains whose aggregate occurrence was highly predictive of CMV seropositivity.
source: By correlating occurrence patterns of public TCRβ chains with cytomegalovirus (CMV) serostatus across a large cohort of healthy individuals, Emerson et al. identified a set of CMV-associated TCR chains whose aggregate occurrence was highly predictive of CMV seropositivity (Emerson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Emerson et al. 2017 study.

claim: MHC proteins in humans are encoded by the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) loci and are among the most polymorphic in the human genome.
source: MHC proteins in humans are encoded by the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) loci and are among the most polymorphic in the human genome (Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Within an individual, six major antigen-presenting proteins are each encoded by polymorphic alleles.
source: Within an individual, six major antigen-presenting proteins are each encoded by polymorphic alleles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HLA genetics.

claim: The set of HLA alleles comprise the individual's HLA type, which is unlikely to be shared with an unrelated individual.
source: The set of these alleles comprise the individual's HLA type, which is unlikely to be shared with an unrelated individual
evidence: This is established knowledge about HLA diversity in populations.

claim: HLA type determines the subset of peptide epitopes presented to T cells for immune surveillance.
source: which determines the subset of peptide epitopes presented to T cells for immune surveillance
evidence: This is established knowledge about HLA function.

claim: The TCR binds to a hybrid molecular surface composed of peptide- and MHC-derived residues.
source: the TCR binds to a hybrid molecular surface composed of peptide- and MHC-derived residues
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about TCR:pMHC interactions.

claim: Population-level studies of TCR-disease association are severely complicated by a dependence on individual HLA type.
source: Thus, population-level studies of TCR-disease association are severely complicated by a dependence on individual HLA type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the established relationship between TCR, HLA, and disease.

claim: The study analyzed occurrence patterns of public TCRs in a cohort of 666 healthy volunteer donors.
source: Here we report an analysis of the occurrence patterns of public TCRs in a cohort of 666 healthy volunteer donors
evidence: This describes the study design and cohort size.

claim: High-resolution HLA typing data at the major class I and class II HLA loci was assembled for the cohort.
source: we have assembled high-resolution HLA typing data at the major class I and class II HLA loci on the same cohort
evidence: This describes the data collected for the study.

claim: Four of the top five most significant clusters appear linked with common pathogens (parvovirus B19, influenza virus, CMV, and Epstein-Barr virus).
source: Four of the top five most significant clusters appear linked with common pathogens (parvovirus B19, influenza virus, CMV, and Epstein-Barr virus)
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis, supported by annotation matches.

claim: The study identified HLA-unrestricted TCR clusters, some likely to be mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells.
source: We also find HLA-unrestricted TCR clusters, some likely to be mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells, which recognize bacterial metabolites presented by non-polymorphic MR1 proteins, rather than pMHC (Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis, with inference about MAIT cell identity.

claim: The global analysis of TCR-HLA association identifies striking variation in association strength across HLA loci.
source: Our global analysis of TCR-HLA association identifies striking variation in association strength across HLA loci
evidence: This is a primary finding from the association analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The analysis identifies statistically significant sequence covariation between the TCR CDR3 loop and the DRB1 allele sequence that preserves charge complementarity at the TCR:pMHC interface.
source: we used our large dataset of HLA-associated TCRβ chains to identify statistically significant sequence covaration between the TCR CDR3 loop and the DRB1 allele sequence that preserves charge complementarity at the TCR:pMHC interface
evidence: This is a primary finding from the covariation analysis presented in Table 2 and Figure 9.

claim: Of the 80 million unique TCRβ chains in the 666 cohort repertoires, about 11 million chains are found in at least two individuals and referred to as public chains.
source: Of the 80 million unique TCRβ chains (defined by V-gene family and CDR3 sequence) in the 666 cohort repertoires, about 11 million chains are found in at least two individuals and referred to here as public chains
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Emerson et al. were able to successfully predict HLA-A and HLA-B allele type and CMV serostatus by learning sets of public TCRβ chains with occurrence patterns that were predictive of these features.
source: (Emerson et al., 2017) demonstrated that this binary occurrence matrix M encodes information on subject genotype and immune history: they were able to successfully predict HLA-A and HLA-B allele type and CMV serostatus by learning sets of public TCRβ chains with occurrence patterns that were predictive of these features.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Emerson et al. 2017 study.

claim: At an approximate family-wise error rate of 0.05, the study identified 28 clusters of co-occurring TCRs over the full cohort, with sizes ranging from 7 to 386 TCRs.
source: At an approximate family-wise error rate of 0.05 (see Materials and methods), we identified 28 clusters of co-occurring TCRs, with sizes ranging from 7 to 386 TCRs (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: The majority of the TCR clusters were strongly associated with at least one HLA allele.
source: Performing this comparison against the occurrence patterns of class I and class II HLA alleles revealed that the majority of the TCR clusters were strongly associated with at least one HLA allele (as depicted for a DRB1*15:01-associated cluster in Figure 3C and summarized in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: One large cluster of TCRs was associated with the TRBJ2-7*02 allele, demonstrating that population diversity in germline allele sets manifests as occurrence pattern clustering.
source: Visual inspection of the CDR3 regions of TCRs in one of these clusters revealed a distinctive 'YV' C-terminal motif that is characteristic of the TRBJ2-7*02 allele (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and indeed the 41 subjects whose repertoires indicated the presence of this genetic variant were exactly the 41 subjects enriched for members of this TCR cluster (Figure 3D). This demonstrated that population diversity in germline allele sets manifests as occurrence pattern clustering.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis with supporting data in Figure 3D.

claim: One large, non-HLA associated TCR cluster represented MAIT cells based on distinctive features including strong preference for TRBV06 family, low numbers of inserted N nucleotides, and skewed age distribution biased toward younger subjects.
source: The other large, non-HLA associated TCR cluster had a number of distinctive features as well: strong preference for the TRBV06 family, followed by TRBV20 and TRBV04 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2); low numbers of inserted 'N' nucleotides; and a skewed age distribution biased toward younger subjects (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). These features, together with the lack of apparent HLA restriction, suggested that this cluster represented an invariant T cell subset, specifically MAIT (mucosal-associated invariant T) cells (Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012; Venturi et al., 2013; Pogorelyy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence from the data analysis.

claim: At a false discovery rate of 0.05, the study was able to assign 16,951 TCRβ sequences to an HLA allele.
source: At a false discovery rate of 0.05 (estimated from shuffling experiments; see Materials and methods), we were able to assign 16,951 TCRβ sequences to an HLA allele (or alleles: DQ and DP alleles were analyzed as αβ pairs, and there were 5 DR/DQ haplotypes whose component alleles were so highly correlated across our cohort that we could not assign TCR associations to individual DR or DQ components; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the HLA association analysis.

claim: Each of the 8 viral epitope-responsive A*02:01-associated TCRβ chains is present in a recent experimental dataset that included tetramer-sorted TCRs positive for these two epitopes.
source: Moreover, each of these 8 TCRβ chains is present in a recent experimental dataset (Dash et al., 2017) that included tetramer-sorted TCRs positive for these two epitopes
evidence: This is a validation finding comparing the study's results to an independent experimental dataset.

claim: HLA-associated TCRs are on average more clonally expanded than a set of background, non-HLA associated TCRs with matching frequencies in the cohort.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, HLA-associated TCRs are on average more clonally expanded than a set of background, non-HLA associated TCRs with matching frequencies in the cohort.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 4A comparing clonal expansion distributions.

claim: HLA-associated TCRs have lower generation probabilities than background TCRs, suggesting that their observed cohort frequencies may be elevated by selection.
source: They also have lower generation probabilities—are harder to make under a simple random model of the VDJ rearrangement process—which suggests that their observed cohort frequencies may be elevated by selection (Figure 4B, see Materials and methods for further details on the calculation of clonal expansion indices and generation probabilities; also see (Pogorelyy et al., 2018)).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 4B, with inference about selection.

claim: HLA-associated TCRs show an excess of lower-probability, clonally expanded TCRs, with this trend appearing stronger for class-I associated TCRs than for class II-associated TCRs.
source: Examination of two-dimensional feature distributions suggests that these shifts are correlated, with HLA-associated TCRs showing an excess of lower-probability, clonally expanded TCRs (Figure 4C); this trend appears stronger for class-I associated TCRs than for class II-associated TCRs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the two-dimensional analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The slope of the correlation between cohort frequency and number of associated TCRs varied dramatically among the HLA loci, with HLA-DRB1 alleles having the largest number of associated TCRs for a given allele frequency and HLA-C alleles having the smallest.
source: What was somewhat more surprising is that the slope of the correlation between cohort frequency and number of associated TCRs varied dramatically among the HLA loci, with HLA-DRB1 alleles having the largest number of associated TCRs for a given allele frequency and HLA-C alleles having the smallest.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The best-fit slope for the five DR/DQ haplotypes (12.2) was roughly the sum of the DR (7.99) and DQ (3.39) slopes, suggesting that these haplotypes were capturing TCRs associated with both the DR and DQ component alleles.
source: The best-fit slope for the five DR/DQ haplotypes (12.2) was roughly the sum of the DR (7.99) and DQ (3.39) slopes, suggesting as expected that these haplotypes were capturing TCRs associated with both the DR and DQ component alleles.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis with inference about the biological meaning.

claim: The smaller rate of TCR association observed at the HLA-C locus could be explained by a relatively lower level of cell surface expression of HLA-C alleles as well as their greater tendency to interact with killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (KIR) on natural killer (NK) cells.
source: The smaller rate of TCR association observed at the HLA-C locus could be explained by a relatively lower level of cell surface expression of HLA-C alleles as well as their greater tendency to interact with killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (KIR) on natural killer (NK) cells (Kaur et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed finding, supported by citation.

claim: 90% of the VDJdb assignments for TCRβ chains present in both the study's dataset and VDJdb matched the study's HLA associations.
source: First, we compared our HLA allele assignments to those given in the VDJdb database (which provides the peptide:MHC target and hence a putative HLA restriction for all entries; [Shugay et al., 2018]) and found that 90% of the VDJdb assignments for TCRβ chains present in both sets matched our associations.
evidence: This is a validation finding comparing the study's results to an external database.

claim: The agreement between the study's HLA associations and VDJdb increases to 96% after filtering for the highest level of supporting evidence (VDJdb score of 3).
source: This agreement increases to 96% after filtering for the highest level of supporting evidence (VDJdb score of 3).
evidence: This is a validation finding showing improved agreement with higher quality data.

claim: TCRβ chains associated with class I MHC molecules are preferentially found in CD8+ populations, while class II-associated TCRs are found in CD4+ populations.
source: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows that if we assign each TCRβ to the class (CD4+ or CD8+) with the higher count, these assignments are largely concordant with the MHC class of its associated HLA allele
evidence: This is a validation finding using independent CD4/CD8 sorted repertoire data.

claim: Using the Holm multiple testing criterion to limit the approximate family-wise error rate to 0.05, the study found a total of 78 significant HLA-restricted TCR clusters.
source: using the Holm multiple testing criterion (Holm, 1979) to limit the approximate family-wise error rate to 0.05, we found a total of 78 significant TCR clusters.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the HLA-restricted clustering analysis.

claim: The top cluster by both size and co-occurrence is an A*24:02-associated group of highly similar TCRβ chains, five of which can be found in a set of 12 TCRβ sequences reported to respond to the parvovirus B19 epitope FYTPLADQF.
source: For example, the top cluster by both size and co-occurrence (Figure 7, upper panels) is an A*24:02-associated group of highly similar TCRβ chains, five of which can be found in a set of 12 TCRβ sequences reported to respond to the parvovirus B19 epitope FYTPLADQF as part of a highly focused CD8+ response to acute B19 infection (Kasprowicz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis with validation from published literature.

claim: The B*08:01-associated cluster #5 appears to be EBV-associated, with four of the TCRβ chains in this cluster matching TCRs annotated as binding to EBV epitopes.
source: Finally, the B*08:01-associated cluster #5 (bottom panels in Figure 8) appears to be EBV-associated: four of the TCRβ chains in this cluster match TCRs annotated as binding to EBV epitopes (two matches for the B*08:01-restricted FLRGRAYGL epitope and two for the B*08:01-restricted RAKFKQLL epitope).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis with annotation matches.

claim: 94% of the Keck120 validation scores and 92% of the Brit86 validation scores are greater than 0, indicating a tendency of the clustered TCRs to co-occur.
source: co-occurrence scores support the validity of the clusterings identified on the discovery cohort: 94% of the Keck120 scores and 92% of the Brit86 scores are greater than 0, indicating a tendency of the clustered TCRs to co-occur (smoothed score distributions are shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a validation finding using independent cohorts.

claim: The class II position 70 correlation was driven largely by HLA-DRB1 alleles, with position 70 correlations of -0.56 versus -0.10 for DR and DQ, respectively, over the full CDR3 and -0.64 vs -0.38 for the non-germline CDR3.
source: Further analysis of the class II correlation suggested that it was driven largely by HLA-DRB1 alleles: position 70 correlations were −0.56 versus −0.10 for DR and DQ, respectively, over the full CDR3 and −0.64 vs −0.38 for the non-germline CDR3.
evidence: This is a finding from further analysis of the covariation data.

claim: The majority of the CMV-associated chains appear to be HLA-associated, having p-values that exceed the FDR 0.05 threshold for HLA association.
source: From this plot we can see that the majority of the CMV-associated chains do appear to be HLA-associated, having p-values that exceed the FDR 0.05 threshold for HLA association.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of CMV-associated TCRs shown in Figure 10A.

claim: For most of the CMV-associated TCRβ chains, CMV association is restricted to the subset of the cohort positive for their associated HLA allele.
source: We see that the majority of the points lie below the y=x line—indicating a stronger CMV-association on the subset of the cohort positive for the associated allele
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The HLA associations of CMV-predictive chains are largely driven by CMV exposure, as evidenced by the lack of significant HLA-association on the CMV-negative cohort subset.
source: Thus, the apparent lack of any significant HLA-association on the CMV-negative cohort subset suggests that the HLA associations of these CMV-predictive chains are largely driven by CMV exposure.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: TCRs with HLA promiscuity may be especially interesting from a diagnostic perspective, since their phenotype associations may be more robust to differences in genetic background.
source: TCRs with HLA promiscuity may be especially interesting from a diagnostic perspective, since their phenotype associations may be more robust to differences in genetic background.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential utility of HLA-promiscuous TCRs.

claim: Several of the most significant HLA-restricted clusters appear linked to common viral pathogens based on sequence matches to experimentally-characterized receptors.
source: Indirect evidence from sequence matches to experimentally-characterized receptors suggests that some of these TCR clusters may reflect hidden immune exposures shared among subsets of the cohort members; indeed, several of the most significant clusters appear linked to common viral pathogens (parvovirus B19, influenza, CMV, and EBV).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis with validation from annotation matches.

claim: The finding by Emerson et al. that there are large numbers of TCRβ chains whose occurrence patterns are strongly associated with specific HLA alleles has been replicated and extended in this work.
source: The finding by Emerson et al.—now replicated and extended in this work—that there are large numbers of TCRβ chains whose occurrence patterns (independent of potential TCRα partners) are strongly associated with specific HLA alleles
evidence: This is a statement about replication of prior findings.

claim: Responses to common pathogens may play a role in selecting TCRβ chains in an HLA-restricted manner.
source: Our observations point to a potential role for responses to common pathogens in selecting some of these chains in an HLA-restricted manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings about pathogen-associated clusters.

claim: Class II loci appear on average to have greater numbers of associated TCRβ chains than class I loci.
source: We also find it interesting that class II loci appear on average to have greater numbers of associated TCRβ chains than class I loci (Figure 5)
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The class II bias in TCR association numbers presumably reflects differences in selection and/or abundance between the CD4+ and CD8+ T cell compartments.
source: presumably this reflects differences in selection and/or abundance between the CD4+ and CD8+ T cell compartments (Sinclair et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed finding, supported by citation.

claim: The lack of sequenced TCRα or paired α/β repertoires for this cohort limits the features that can be detected and may introduce bias into some of the study's conclusions.
source: The lack of sequenced TCRα or paired α/β repertoires for this cohort limits the features we can detect and may introduce bias into some of our conclusions.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: It is likely that many TCRs that are associated with specific immune exposures when considered as paired TCR chains are not detectably associated with those exposures when analyzing only the α or β chain alone.
source: It is likely that many TCRs that are associated with specific immune exposures when considered as paired TCR chains are not detectably associated with those exposures (or with other TCRs responding to those exposures) when analyzing only the α or β chain alone
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of single-chain analysis.

claim: Two of the EBV-annotated clusters contain TCRβ chains also seen in the context of rheumatoid arthritis, suggesting possible cross-reactivity between pathogen and autoimmune epitopes.
source: As an example, two of our EBV-annotated clusters contain TCRβ chains also seen in the context of rheumatoid arthritis: cross-reactivity between pathogen and autoimmune epitopes may mean that TCR clusters discovered on the basis of common infections also provide information relevant in the context of autoimmunity.
evidence: This is a finding from the annotation analysis with speculation about cross-reactivity.

claim: 592 TCRβ nucleotide sequences were removed from the analysis as potential cross-contamination artifacts.
source: We elected to remove all TCRβ nucleotide sequences whose sharing rates put them outside the decision boundary indicated by the black line in Figure 11, which eliminated the vast majority of the artifactual variants as well as a handful of other highly shared, low-probability sequences (592 nucleotide sequences in total were removed).
evidence: This describes a data quality control step taken in the analysis.

claim: HLA genotyping was performed and confirmed by molecular means, including sequence specific oligonucleotide probe typing (SSOP), Sanger sequencing (SBT) or next generation sequencing (NGS).
source: HLA genotyping was performed and confirmed by molecular means, including sequence specific oligonucleotide probe typing (SSOP), Sanger sequencing (SBT) or next generation sequencing (NGS) (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the methods used for HLA typing.

claim: HLA typing data availability varied across loci, with HLA-A (629 subjects), HLA-B (630 subjects), HLA-C (629 subjects), HLA-DRB1 (630 subjects), HLA-DQA1 (522 subjects), HLA-DQB1 (630 subjects), HLA-DPA1 (606 subjects), and HLA-DPB1 (472 subjects).
source: HLA typing data availability varied across loci as follows: HLA-A (629 subjects), HLA-B (630 subjects), HLA-C (629 subjects), HLA-DRB1 (630 subjects), HLA-DQA1 (522 subjects), HLA-DQB1 (630 subjects), HLA-DPA1 (606 subjects), and HLA-DPB1 (472 subjects).
evidence: This describes the data availability for the study.

claim: The study implemented a version of the probabilistic model proposed by Walczak and co-workers to assign generation probabilities to TCRβ chains.
source: We implemented a version of the probabilistic model proposed by Walczak and co-workers (Murugan et al., 2012) in order to assign to each public TCRβ chain (defined by a V-gene family and a CDR3 amino acid sequence) a generation probability, Pgen
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study.
